column2: But when the ship had left the stream of the river Okeanos,
and came to the wave of the wide-pathed sea
and the Aeaean island, where are the dwelling of early-born Dawn
and her dancing-floors and the risings of Helios,
going there we beached the ship on the sands,
and ourselves too went out onto the breaking edge of the sea;
and there we fell asleep and waited for divine Dawn.
And when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
then I sent comrades ahead to the house of Circe
to bring the corpse, the dead Elpenor.
And quickly cutting logs, where the shore projected furthest,
we buried him, grieving, shedding warm tears.
And when the corpse was burned and the dead man's armour,
having heaped a mound and drawn a pillar up on it,
we fixed the well-made oar on the top of the mound.
We attended to each of these things; nor did we, having come
from Hades, escape Circe's notice, but very quickly
she came, having dressed herself; and with her handmaids carried
bread and much meat and gleaming red wine.
And she, standing in the middle, spoke, bright among goddesses:

Hardy ones, who alive went down to the house of Hades,
22	twice-dying, when other men die once.
23	But come, eat food and drink wine
24	here for the whole day; and when dawn appears
25	you shall sail; and I shall show you the way and
26	point out each thing, so that you do not through some grievous contrivance
27	on sea or on land suffer pain and meet with woe.
So she spoke, and our proud heart obeyed.
So then for the whole day until the sun went down
we sat feasting on endless meat and sweet wine;
and when the sun went down and darkness came on,
they lay down to sleep beside the stern cables of the ship,
and she, taking me by the hand apart from my dear comrades,
seated me and lay beside me and questioned me on each thing;
and I told her everything in due order.
And then lady Circe addressed me with words:

These things are all thus brought to an end; but you listen,
38	as I tell you, and a god himself will remind you.
39	First you will come to the Sirens, who bewitch
40	all men, whoever comes to them.
41	Whoever in ignorance draws near and hears the voice
42	of the Sirens, for him no wife and infant children
43	stand by him when he has come home, nor rejoice,
44	but the Sirens bewitch him with clear-toned song,
45	sitting in a meadow, and around them is a great heap of bones
46	of rotting men, and the skins shrivel round them.
47	But drive past, and anoint the ears of your comrades
48	with kneaded honey-sweet wax, lest any
49	of the others hear; but you yourself, if you wish to hear,
50	let them bind you in the swift ship hand and foot,
51	upright in the mast-step, and from it let the ropes be fastened,
52	so that you may hear the Sirens' voice with delight.
53	And if you beg your comrades and bid them loose you,
54	let them then bind you with still more bonds.
55	But when your comrades have driven past them,
56	then I shall not tell you any longer continuously
57	which way will be your road, but you yourself
58	must decide in your heart; I shall tell you of both sides.
59	For on one side are overhanging rocks, and against them
60	the great wave of dark-eyed Amphitrite roars;
61	Wandering Rocks the blessed gods call them.
62	By there not even winged things pass, nor timid
63	doves, which bring ambrosia to father Zeus,
64	but the smooth rock always takes one of them away;
65	but the father sends in another to make up the number.
66	Past there no ship of men has yet escaped, whichever comes,
67	but together the planks of ships and the bodies of men
68	the waves of the sea carry, and storms of destructive fire.
69	Only that one sea-going ship sailed past,
70	Argo, known to all, sailing from Aietes.
71	And she too would quickly have been dashed there against the great rocks,
72	but Hera sent her past, since Jason was dear to her.
73	And of the two crags, one reaches the broad heaven
74	with a sharp peak, and a dark cloud
75	surrounds it; this never clears, nor does clear sky
76	hold its peak either in summer or in harvest-time.
77	Nor could a mortal man climb it nor set foot on it,
78	not even if he had twenty hands and feet;
79	for the rock is smooth, like something polished all round.
80	And in the middle of the crag is a misty cave,
81	turned towards the gloom, to Erebos, where you
82	will steer your hollow ship, glorious Odysseus.
83	Nor could a vigorous man from the hollow ship
84	shooting with a bow reach the hollow cave.
85	There inside dwells Scylla, yelping terribly.
86	Her voice indeed is as great as that of a newborn puppy,
87	but she herself is an evil monster; and no one would be glad
88	to see her, not even if a god met her.
89	Of her there are twelve feet, all dangling,
90	and six very long necks, and on each
91	a dreadful head, and in them three rows of teeth,
92	thick and close, full of black death.
93	In the middle she is sunk down in the hollow cave,
94	but she thrusts her heads outside the dread pit,
95	and there she fishes, groping round the crag,
96	for dolphins and dogfish, and if anywhere she can take a bigger
97	monster, of the countless ones that loud-moaning Amphitrite feeds.
98	By her no sailors yet can boast
99	that they have escaped unharmed with their ship; for with each head she carries
100	off a man, snatching him from the dark-prowed ship.
101	And the other crag you will see lower, Odysseus,
102	close to each other; you could even shoot an arrow across.
103	On it is a great wild fig-tree, flourishing with leaves;
104	and beneath it divine Charybdis sucks down the black water.
105	For three times a day she sends it up, and three times she sucks it down
106	dreadfully; may you not be there when she sucks;
107	for not even the Earth-shaker could save you from the evil.
108	But keeping very close to Scylla's crag, quickly
109	drive the ship past, since it is much better
110	to miss six comrades from the ship than all together.
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:

Come now, goddess, tell me this unerringly,
113	whether I might escape the destructive Charybdis,
114	and yet ward off the other when she harms my comrades.
So I spoke, and she at once answered, bright among goddesses:

Hardy man, so again the deeds of war are your concern
117	and toil; will you not yield even to the immortal gods?
118	She is not mortal, but an immortal evil,
119	dread and grievous and savage and not to be fought;
120	nor is there any defence; to flee from her is best.
121	For if you linger arming yourself beside the rock,
122	I fear lest she rush out again and reach you
123	with as many heads, and take as many men.
124	But drive very vigorously, and call on Crataiis,
125	the mother of Scylla, who bore her as a bane to mortals;
126	she will then stop her from rushing out again.
127	And you will come to the island of Thrinacia; and there many
128	cattle of Helios graze, and fat sheep,
129	seven herds of cattle, and as many fair flocks of sheep,
130	fifty in each. And no offspring is born of them,
131	nor do they ever die. And goddesses are their shepherds,
132	fair-tressed nymphs, Phaethusa and Lampetie,
133	whom divine Neaira bore to Helios Hyperion.
134	These their lady mother, when she had borne and reared them,
135	sent to the island of Thrinacia to dwell far away,
136	to guard their father's sheep and curved-horned cattle.
137	If you leave these unharmed and think of your homecoming,
138	you may yet reach Ithaca, though suffering evils;
139	but if you harm them, then I foretell destruction
140	for your ship and your comrades; and even if you yourself escape,
141	late you will return in evil plight, having lost all your comrades.
So she spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
Then she went away up the island, bright among goddesses;
and I, going to the ship, urged on my comrades
to embark themselves and to loose the stern cables;
and they quickly went aboard and sat at the oars.
And sitting in order they struck the grey sea with their oars.
And for us from behind the dark-prowed ship
a fair wind that filled the sail she sent, a good companion,
Circe of the fair tresses, a dread goddess with human speech.
At once, having seen to each of the tackle throughout the ship,
we sat; and the wind and the helmsman steered her.
Then I spoke among my comrades, grieved at heart:

Friends, it is not right that one or two alone should know
155	the oracles that Circe, bright among goddesses, told me;
156	but I shall tell them, so that knowing we may either die
157	or, avoiding death and doom, escape.
158	First she bade us avoid the voice of the marvellous
159	Sirens, and their flowery meadow.
160	Me alone she bade hear their voice; but bind me
161	in grievous bonds, so that I may stay fast there,
162	upright in the mast-step, and from it let the ropes be fastened.
163	And if I beg you and bid you to loose me,
164	then you are to squeeze me with still more bonds.
Thus I was telling each thing and making it plain to my comrades;
and meanwhile the well-built ship quickly arrived
at the island of the Sirens; for a harmless wind urged her on.
Then at once the wind ceased and a calm
set in, windless, and a god lulled the waves.
And my comrades, standing up, furled the sails of the ship
and put them in the hollow ship, and sitting at the oars
they whitened the water with their polished fir blades.
But I, with the sharp bronze, cut a great wheel of wax
into small pieces and squeezed them with my stout hands;
and quickly the wax grew warm, since strong force pressed it
and the beam of lord Helios Hyperion's son;
and in order I anointed the ears of all my comrades.
And they bound me in the ship together hand and foot,
upright in the mast-step, and fastened the ropes from it;
and themselves sitting they struck the grey sea with their oars.
But when we were as far off as a shout carries,
driving swiftly, the swift ship did not escape them
as she moved near, and they raised a clear-toned song:

Come here, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans,
185	bring your ship to rest, that you may hear our voice.
186	For no one yet has passed this way in a black ship
187	before hearing the honey-voiced sound from our mouths,
188	but he goes on delighted and knowing more.
189	For we know all that in broad Troy
190	the Argives and Trojans suffered by the gods' will,
191	and we know whatever happens on the much-nourishing earth.
So they said, sending forth a beautiful voice; and my heart
wished to hear, and I bade my comrades loose me,
nodding with my brows; but they bent forward and rowed.
And at once Perimedes and Eurylochus, standing up,
bound me with more bonds and squeezed me tighter.
But when they had passed them, and no longer after that
did we hear the voice of the Sirens or their song,
at once my trusty comrades took away the wax
with which I had anointed their ears, and released me from the bonds.
But when we were leaving the island, at once then
I saw smoke and a great wave, and heard a roar.
And in their fear the oars flew from their hands,
and everything boomed along the stream; and the ship
stopped there, since they no longer plied the long oars with their hands.
But I, going through the ship, urged on my comrades
with honeyed words, standing by each man:

Friends, we are not at all unacquainted with evils;
209	this is no greater evil that comes upon us than when the Cyclops
210	penned us in the hollow cave with his mighty strength;
211	but even from there, by my courage, counsel and wit,
212	we escaped, and I think we shall remember this too some day.
213	Now come, as I say, let us all obey.
214	You, sitting at the benches, strike the deep surf of the sea
215	with your oars, in case Zeus somehow
216	may grant us to escape this destruction and get away.
217	And to you, helmsman, I give this order; but lay it up in your heart,
218	since you handle the steering-oar of the hollow ship.
219	Keep the ship clear of this smoke and wave,
220	and make for the crag, lest she slip away from you
221	over there, and you cast us into evil.
So I spoke, and they quickly obeyed my words.
But of Scylla I said no more, an irremediable grief,
lest in fear my comrades might cease
from rowing, and huddle themselves inside.
And then I forgot Circe's grievous command,
since she had not bidden me to arm myself;
but I put on my famous armour and taking two long
spears in my hands, I stepped onto the decking of the ship
at the prow; for from there I expected first to see
rocky Scylla, who brought woe to my comrades.
Nor could I see her anywhere, and my eyes grew weary
as I looked everywhere towards the misty rock.
We sailed up the narrow strait lamenting;
on one side was Scylla, and on the other divine Charybdis
dreadfully sucked down the salt water of the sea.
When she vomited it up, like a cauldron on a great fire
she all seethed, stirred up, and the spray on high
fell on the tops of both crags;
but when she gulped down the salt water of the sea,
she appeared all stirred up within, and the rock around
roared terribly, and beneath the earth appeared
dark with sand; and pale fear seized them.
We looked towards her, fearing destruction;
but meanwhile Scylla took from the hollow ship six
comrades, who were the strongest in hands and might.
And looking at the swift ship and at my comrades,
already I noticed their feet and hands above
being lifted high; and they called to me,
calling me by name, then for the last time, grieved at heart.
As when on a projecting headland a fisherman with a very long rod,
casting a bait for the little fishes,
lets down into the sea the horn of a field ox,
and then catching one gasping flings it ashore,
so they gasping were lifted up towards the rocks;
and there at her doors she devoured them, shrieking,
stretching out their hands to me in dread conflict;
that was the most pitiable thing I saw with my eyes
of all that I suffered, searching out the paths of the sea.
But when we had escaped the rocks and dread Charybdis
and Scylla, at once then to the blameless island of the god
we came; and there were the fair broad-browed cattle
and many fat sheep of Hyperion Helios.
Then, while I was still at sea in the black ship,
I heard the lowing of cattle being penned
and the bleating of sheep; and the word fell into my heart
of the blind seer, Theban Teiresias,
and of Aeaean Circe, who charged me very much
to avoid the island of Helios who gladdens mortals.
Then I spoke among my comrades, grieved at heart:

Hear my words, comrades, though you suffer evils,
272	so that I may tell you the prophecies of Teiresias
273	and of Aeaean Circe, who charged me very much
274	to avoid the island of Helios who gladdens mortals;
275	for there, she said, the most dreadful evil would be for us.
276	But drive the black ship past the island.
So I spoke, and their dear hearts were broken.
And at once Eurylochus answered me with hateful word:

You are hardy, Odysseus; you have great strength, and your limbs
280	do not tire; surely all of you is made of iron,
281	who do not allow your comrades, worn out with toil and sleep,
282	to set foot on land, where again
283	on the sea-girt island we might prepare a pleasant supper,
284	but bid us wander thus through the swift night,
285	driven away from the island on the misty sea.
286	And from nights come harsh winds, destroyers of ships;
287	where could one escape sheer destruction,
288	if suddenly a gust of wind should come,
289	either of the South or the stormy West, which most
290	wreck ships even against the will of the lord gods?
291	But come now, let us obey the black night
292	and prepare supper, staying by the swift ship,
293	and in the morning let us go aboard and put out on the broad sea.
So spoke Eurylochus, and the other comrades assented.
And then I knew that some god was devising evils,
and I spoke to him winged words:

Eurylochus, you certainly force me, being alone.
298	But come now, all swear me a strong oath:
299	if we find any herd of cattle or great flock of sheep,
300	that no one through evil recklessness
301	will kill an ox or any sheep; but at ease
302	eat the food which immortal Circe gave.
So I spoke, and they at once swore, as I bade.
But when they had sworn and completed the oath,
we stopped the well-built ship in the hollow harbour
near sweet water, and my comrades disembarked
from the ship, and then skilfully prepared supper.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
remembering then they wept for their dear comrades,
whom Scylla had eaten, seizing them from the hollow ship;
and as they wept sweet sleep came upon them.
But when it was the third part of the night, and the stars had turned,
cloud-gathering Zeus roused against us a violent wind
with a marvellous storm, and covered with clouds
land and sea alike; and night rushed down from heaven.
And when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
we moored the ship, drawing her into a hollow cave.
There were the fair dancing-floors of the nymphs and their seats;
and then, calling an assembly, I spoke a word among them:

Friends, in the swift ship there is food and drink
321	there is, so let us keep away from the cattle, lest we suffer;
322	for these cattle and fat sheep belong to a dread god,
323	Helios, who oversees all things and hears all things.
So I spoke, and their proud heart obeyed.
For a whole month the South wind blew without ceasing, and no other
of the winds came after, except the East and the South.
And they, as long as they had bread and red wine,
kept away from the cattle, longing for life.
But when all the provisions of the ship were used up,
then they went after game, wandering by necessity,
fish and birds, whatever came to their hands,
with curved hooks, and hunger wore down their bellies;
then I went away up the island, to pray
to the gods, in case one might show me a way to return.
But when, going through the island, I had got away from my comrades,
having washed my hands, where there was shelter from the wind,
I prayed to all the gods who hold Olympus;
and they poured sweet sleep upon my eyelids.
And Eurylochus began an evil counsel among my comrades:

Hear my words, comrades, though you suffer evils.
341	All deaths are hateful to wretched mortals,
342	but to die of hunger and meet one's fate is most pitiable.
343	But come, let us drive off the best of the cattle of Helios
344	and sacrifice to the immortals who hold the broad heaven.
345	And if we reach Ithaca, our fatherland,
346	at once we shall build for Helios Hyperion
347	a rich temple, and place in it many fine offerings.
348	But if, angered over his straight-horned cattle,
349	he wishes to destroy our ship, and the other gods follow,
350	I would rather lose my life once, gaping at a wave,
351	than be slowly pinched to death while on a desert island.
So spoke Eurylochus, and the other comrades assented.
And at once, driving off the best of the cattle of Helios
from near by, for not far from the dark-prowed ship
the fair curved-horned broad-browed cattle were grazing;
they stood around them and prayed to the gods,
plucking tender leaves from a high-crested oak;
for they had no white barley on the well-benched ship.
But when they had prayed and slaughtered and flayed,
they cut out the thigh-bones and covered them with fat,
making a double fold, and laid raw pieces on them.
Nor had they wine to pour on the burning sacrifices,
but pouring libations with water they roasted all the entrails.
And when the thighs were burned and they had tasted the innards,
they cut up the rest and pierced it on spits.
And then sweet sleep rushed from my eyelids,
and I went to the swift ship and the sea-shore.
But when, going, I was already near the curved ship,
then the sweet savour of fat came around me.
And groaning I cried out to the immortal gods:
And swift to Helios Hyperion came a messenger,
long-robed Lampetie, saying that we had killed his cattle.
And at once she spoke among the immortals, angry at heart:

Father Zeus and other blessed gods who are for ever,
378	punish the comrades of Odysseus son of Laertes,
379	who insolently killed my cattle, in which I
380	rejoiced as I went to the starry heaven,
381	and when I turned back again to earth from heaven.
382	And if they do not pay me fitting recompense for the cattle,
383	I shall go down to Hades and shine among the dead.
And answering him cloud-gathering Zeus said:

Helios, you go on shining among the immortals
386	and for mortal men upon the grain-giving earth;
387	and of these men I shall soon strike their swift ship with a bright
388	thunderbolt and shatter it small in the midst of the wine-dark sea.
This I heard from fair-haired Calypso;
and she said she herself had heard it from Hermes the guide.
But when I had come down to the ship and the sea,
I rebuked them, one after another, standing by, nor could we
find any remedy; for the cattle were already dead.
And to them at once then the gods showed portents:
the hides crawled, and the flesh bellowed about the spits,
roast and raw, and there was a voice as of cattle.
For six days then my trusty comrades
feasted, having driven off the best of the cattle of Helios;
but when Zeus son of Kronos brought the seventh day,
then the wind ceased raging with its storm,
and we quickly embarked and put out on the broad sea,
setting up the mast and hoisting the white sails.
But when we left the island, and no other land
appeared, but heaven and sea,
then the son of Kronos set a dark cloud
over the hollow ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it.
And she ran not very long; for quickly came
shrieking Zephyrus, raging with a great storm,
and the blast of wind broke the forestays of the mast,
both; and the mast fell backward, and all the tackle
poured into the bilge. And it on the stern of the ship
struck the helmsman's head, and crushed all the bones
of his head together; and he like a diver
fell from the deck, and his proud spirit left his bones.
And Zeus thundered at once and hurled a thunderbolt at the ship;
and she shook all over, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus,
and was filled with sulphur, and my comrades fell from the ship.
And they like sea-crows around the black ship
were carried on the waves, and the god took away their return.
But I kept moving through the ship, until the surge
loosened the sides from the keel, and the wave carried it bare,
and broke off the mast against the keel. And on it
was thrown a backstay, made of ox-hide;
with this I bound together both, keel and mast,
and sitting on them I was carried by the baleful winds.
Then indeed Zephyrus ceased raging with its storm,
and the South wind came quickly, bringing pains to my heart,
that I might measure again the destructive Charybdis.
All night I was carried, and at sunrise
I came to the crag of Scylla and dread Charybdis.
She was sucking down the salt water of the sea;
but I, lifted high to the tall wild fig-tree,
clung to it like a bat. And nowhere could I
either get a firm footing or climb on;
for the roots were far off, and the branches hung aloft,
long and great, and overshadowed Charybdis.
Steadfastly I held on, until she should vomit up again
the mast and keel; and to my longing they came
late; at the time when a man rises from the assembly for supper,
judging many disputes of litigating young men,
at that time those timbers appeared from Charybdis.
And I let my feet and hands drop from above,
and plumped down in the middle beside the very long timbers,
and sitting on them I paddled with my hands.
And Scylla the father of men and gods no longer allowed
me to see; for I should not have escaped sheer destruction.
From there for nine days I was carried, and on the tenth night
the gods brought me to the island of Ogygia, where Calypso
dwells, fair-tressed, a dread goddess with human speech,
who loved me and cared for me. Why do I tell you this?
For already yesterday I told it in the house
to you and your mighty wife; and it is hateful to me
to tell again what has been plainly told.
